prompt: Which of these is an event, in the sense of this lesson?

choices.text: Reserve one copy of bk-03 for this customer
choices.why: That is a command: it is addressed to one system and it is allowed to fail.

choices.text: Recife has six copies of bk-03
choices.why: That is state, a snapshot that is overwritten the moment it changes.

choices.text: One copy of bk-03 was sold
choices.why: Right. Past tense, already happened, and nobody is asked to do anything.

choices.text: Send the receipt for sale nat-000002 to the customer by email
choices.why: An instruction to one system to act is a command, whatever it is about.

prompt: A shop's system only keeps a table saying how many copies of each book it has now. What is lost that a list of events would have kept?

choices.text: The current number of copies of each book
choices.why: That is exactly what the table keeps.

choices.text: How the number got there: which sales, deliveries and counts, and when
choices.why: Right. State answers how many now and forgets how we got here.

choices.text: Nothing, because the table and the events say the same thing
choices.why: State is rebuilt from events, never the other way round.

choices.text: The prices
choices.why: A table of stock could carry prices too; what it cannot carry is its own history.

prompt: A thin event carries only the sale's id, and the loyalty system looks the rest up in the shop's database. It handles a sale that was stuck on a till for two hours, and the price changed in between. What does it see?

choices.text: The price the customer paid
choices.why: The database holds the row as it is now, not as it was when the sale was rung up.

choices.text: An error, because the event is too old
choices.why: Nothing refuses it; the lookup works and returns today's row.

choices.text: Today's price, which the sale never charged
choices.why: Right. A thin event makes every reader depend on what the source says now.

choices.text: Both prices, because the database keeps a history of every change it has made
choices.why: A table keeps its current rows; a history of changes is what a log is.

prompt: A reader of a log reads records 0 to 9. What happens to those ten records?

choices.text: They stay where they are, for every reader
choices.why: Right. Reading moves the reader's own place and changes nothing in the log.

choices.text: They are deleted, because they have been delivered to a reader
choices.why: That is what a queue does. A log keeps what was written.

choices.text: They are marked as read, and from then on the other readers skip them
choices.why: The log does not know who read what; each reader keeps its own place.

choices.text: They move to the end of the log, behind the newer records
choices.why: Nothing in a log ever moves; offsets are for good.

prompt: A log has records at offsets 0 to 41. What offset will the next appended record get?
In minilog.py, where is the information about how far the loyalty reader has read?

choices.text: In a field written into each record of the log
choices.why: Records are never edited after they are appended.

choices.text: In a file of its own beside the log, holding the next offset
choices.why: Right. demo.log.loyalty, one per reader, and the log knows nothing about it.

choices.text: Nowhere: every read starts again from offset 0
choices.why: The second read of the stock reader printed nothing, so something remembered.

choices.text: In the log's first line
choices.why: The first line is record 0, a sale like any other.

prompt: minilog.py prints a record and then writes the reader's place. The program is killed between the two. What happens on the next read?
hint: Which file holds the old number?

choices.text: The record is skipped
choices.why: Skipping would need the place written before the record was printed.

choices.text: Nothing different from a normal run
choices.why: The place file still holds the old offset, so the reader starts there.

choices.text: The record is printed again
choices.why: Right. Doing the work before recording the place costs a duplicate after a crash.

choices.text: The log is corrupted and refuses to open
choices.why: The log file was not being written; only the reader's place was.

prompt: In Kafka, the position a reader has recorded for itself in a partition is called a committed ___.
hint: The same word as a record's position.

prompt: balance.py prints 6 for Recife. Where was that number stored before the program ran?

choices.text: In the last line of stock.log, which holds the latest stock
choices.why: The last line is a sale of one copy; the 6 is worked out from all eight lines.

choices.text: In a table that balance.py saves and updates on every run of the program
choices.why: balance.py starts from an empty dictionary every time.

choices.text: In the place file of the stock reader
choices.why: A place file holds an offset, not a stock.

choices.text: Nowhere; it is computed from the events each time
choices.why: Right. The table is the fold of the log, done again on each run.

prompt: The stock system had a bug for a week: it subtracted deliveries instead of adding them. The events of that week are still in the log. How is the stock put right?

choices.text: Fix apply and fold the log again from the start
choices.why: Right. With the log kept, the table is a cache that is rebuilt.

choices.text: Edit the delivery events so that their quantities are negative
choices.why: Events are not edited, and the deliveries were right; the code was wrong.

choices.text: Count every shelf again, since the week's numbers are gone for good
choices.why: They are gone only in a system that kept nothing but the table.

choices.text: Delete the week from the log
choices.why: That throws away the very events that rebuild the right numbers.

prompt: Match each idea to what it means.

pairs.right: a stream folded up, latest value per key
walking a list while carrying one value

right_distractors: a copy of the log on another machine

prompt: The Recife stock count reaches the log after the morning's sales instead of before them. What did balance.py print for Recife?

choices.text: An error about the order of the events
choices.why: Nothing in the fold checks order. That is the danger.

choices.text: 6, the same as before
choices.why: 6 came from the right order. The count, applied last, replaced it.

choices.text: 4, which looks plausible and is wrong
choices.why: Right. The shelf as it was at 08:50, applied at the end of the morning.
−1 appeared in the middle of the trace, not at the end.

prompt: A shelf is counted at 5. Then 2 copies are sold and 4 are received. If the count arrives last instead of first, what stock does the fold end with?
hint: What does a count do to the number before it?

prompt: Which pair of events gives the same stock whichever order they arrive in?

choices.text: A count of 4 and a sale of 1
choices.why: 3 one way, 4 the other: the count replaces the number.

choices.text: A delivery of 6 and a sale of 2
choices.why: Right. Adding and subtracting commute; +4 either way.

choices.text: A count of 4 and a delivery of 6
choices.why: 10 one way, 4 the other.

choices.text: Two counts with different numbers
choices.why: Whichever comes last wins, so the order decides the result.

prompt: Rearranging stock.log so that all of Olinda's events come first left the result unchanged. Why?

choices.text: balance.py sorts the events by time before folding
choices.why: It reads them in the order of the file, as the trace shows.

choices.text: The order inside each shop was kept
choices.why: Right. No Olinda event touches Recife's row, so only each shop's own order counts.

choices.text: grep puts lines back in their original order
choices.why: It printed every Olinda line before every other line, which is a new order.

choices.text: Olinda's events all commute with each other
choices.why: Olinda's count does not commute with its sale; their order was simply kept.

prompt: Why does a single total order over every event limit how much a log takes per second?

choices.text: Every write has to go through the one place that decides the order
choices.why: Right. Or two places agree on each write, which is a round trip per event.

choices.text: Hashing every key takes time that grows with the number of events in the log
choices.why: A hash costs nanoseconds; it is how order per key avoids the limit.

choices.text: Records kept in order take more disk than records kept in any order
choices.why: Order costs no bytes; it costs coordination.

choices.text: Readers have to read every record twice
choices.why: Readers are not involved; the limit is on the writing side.

prompt: The tills key their events by shop. A transfer moves five copies of bk-03 from Recife to Olinda. What keeps it in order with both shops' other events?

choices.text: One event keyed by recife, since the copies leave from there
choices.why: It is then in order with Recife's events and with none of Olinda's.

choices.text: One event keyed by the book, which both shops share
choices.why: A different key means a different place, in order with neither shop.

choices.text: One event with no key, so that it reaches everybody
choices.why: With no key it keeps order with nothing at all.

choices.text: Two events, one per shop, each keyed by its own shop
choices.why: Right. Each shop's row gets its own event, in order with that shop's sales.

prompt: Kafka's promise about order: within one ___, records are read in the order they were written.
A recommendations system is built a year after the tills started writing to the log. What does it get?

choices.text: Only the sales written from the moment it first connects to the log
choices.why: That is a queue. A new log reader starts wherever it chooses.

choices.text: Every sale the log still holds, from its first offset
choices.why: Right, as far back as the log has kept them, which lesson 3 sets.

choices.text: Copies the tills send again
choices.why: The tills know nothing about readers, new or old.

choices.text: A summary table of the past year, built by the log instead of the events
choices.why: The log holds events; a table is something a reader builds.

prompt: Six tills each call five systems directly. How many connections is that? (With a log it would be eleven.)
Image resizing: each uploaded image has to be resized once, by whichever worker is free, and nobody will ever need the request again. Which fits better?

choices.text: A log, since every worker reads every message
choices.why: Every worker reading every image would resize each one many times.

choices.text: A log, so the requests are kept for replay
choices.why: Nobody needs them again; keeping them buys nothing here.

choices.text: A queue: each message goes to one free worker and is deleted when done
choices.why: Right. Work done once by whoever is free is a queue's job.

choices.text: Neither: the uploader calls one worker directly
choices.why: Then the uploader has to know which worker is free, and wait when none is.

prompt: Which event name follows the advice of this lesson?

choices.text: update-stock
choices.why: An instruction to one reader: a command in disguise.

choices.text: book-sold
choices.why: Right. Past tense, and it names the fact that happened.

choices.text: sale-updated
choices.why: Past tense, but it says only that something changed, not what.

choices.text: send-receipt
choices.why: An order to do something, with one intended reader.

prompt: Why does every event need an id written by whoever created it?

choices.text: Kafka refuses to store a message that has no id field in its value
choices.why: Kafka accepts any bytes; the id is for the readers.

choices.text: The offset already identifies it, and an id would only repeat it
choices.why: A duplicate sent twice gets two offsets, so the offset cannot spot it.

choices.text: Duplicates happen, and the id spots a second copy
choices.why: Right. Two identical sales in one second differ only by their ids.

choices.text: It sorts the events in time
choices.why: Time is a separate field, at; ids are not timestamps.

prompt: The tills' sale has these fields: sale, shop, book, qty, cents, at. Which of this lesson's rules does it already meet? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A unique id
choices.why: Yes: sale, such as nat-000002.

choices.text: The time it happened, inside
choices.why: Yes: at, from the till's clock.

choices.text: A declared shape or version
choices.why: Missing; lesson 6 adds it.

choices.text: A type field naming the event
choices.why: There is none; the topic sales names it.

prompt: Put the steps of a reader in minilog.py in the order the code does them.
items: read the offset from its place file, or start at 0
open the log and skip records before that offset
print each record from there to the end
write the next offset to its place file

prompt: A system keeps the stock of every book per shop and must never show a number that did not exist. Its events come from tills keyed by shop. Which change would break that?

choices.text: Keying by shop and book together, one key per row of the stock table
choices.why: Every row still gets all of its events in one log, in order.

choices.text: Sending events with no key, so they are spread over the logs
choices.why: Right. A shop's count and sales then sit in different logs with no order between them.

choices.text: Adding a new reader that starts from offset 0
choices.why: Readers do not change the log or each other.

choices.text: Writing events in fat form instead of thin
choices.why: Fat or thin is about what an event carries, not its order.
